issues.legal_issue: A direction to grant fresh mining leases does not permit the State to satisfy that direction by renewing expired leases.
material_facts: A prior final judgment held that the leases had expired and directed the State to decide how to grant mining leases in the future.
The State granted second renewals rather than granting fresh leases.
The prior judgment had been made with the existing second-renewal applications and related payments in view.
issues.conclusion: The State was required to grant fresh leases, not second renewals; the second renewals were contrary to the prior judgment and were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of a judicial direction is determined in its context. Here, the declaration and directions in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738, required fresh grants and did not authorize renewals of expired leases. Although renewal may in some contexts amount to a fresh grant, a direction to grant a fresh lease is not a direction to renew an expired lease. The Court also distinguished the interim direction in Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499. The State’s grant of leases must comply with the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and constitutional requirements.

rule.if: challenge_to_second_renewal and leases_expired and prior_judgment_required_fresh_grants and state_granted_renewals

predicates.challenge_to_second_renewal: A proceeding challenges the validity of second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.leases_expired: The mining leases had expired before the State made its later decisions.
predicates.prior_judgment_required_fresh_grants: A prior final judgment directed the State to make fresh grants rather than continue the expired leases by renewal.
predicates.state_granted_renewals: The State granted renewals of the expired leases instead of making fresh grants.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges second renewals, the leases had expired, a prior final judgment required fresh grants, and the State granted renewals, the renewals are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The Constitution does not require every allocation of a natural resource to be made by auction, although a decision to use another method remains subject to judicial review.
material_facts: The State’s policy contemplated granting mining leases without competitive bidding, and the dispute concerned the allocation of a natural resource other than spectrum.
The Court considered that the mining activity principally served private commercial profit and lacked an evident social or welfare purpose.
The Court did not finally adjudicate whether the State’s decision not to auction fresh leases was arbitrary, and did not quash that decision on this ground.
issues.conclusion: The State was not under a constitutional obligation to grant fresh mining leases by auction. Auction is generally preferable for commercial allocation of natural resources, but it is not constitutionally mandatory in every case; the State’s choice remains reviewable under Article 14. The Court did not finally decide whether the State’s non-auction policy was arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, (2012) 10 SCC 1, held that auction is not the only constitutionally permissible method for allocating natural resources and that Article 14 does not prescribe a single economic policy. It also held that non-auction methods remain reviewable for arbitrariness and fairness, particularly where scarce resources are allocated to private commercial interests without a social or welfare purpose. The Court discussed Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, (2012) 3 SCC 1, Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary, (2014) 9 SCC 516, and M/s Ajar Enterprises Private Limited v. Satyanarayan Somani, 2017 (10) SCALE 346. Article 39(b) is relevant to whether distribution serves the common good. The Court also noted the State’s authority to choose a lawful method under the MMDR Act and its rules.

predicates.natural_resource_allocation_review: A proceeding examines a public authority’s choice of method for allocating a natural resource.
predicates.resource_is_not_spectrum: The resource being allocated is not spectrum.

issues.definition: When a proceeding examines allocation of a natural resource other than spectrum, auction is not constitutionally mandatory.

issues.legal_issue: A second renewal is invalid when the State grants it hastily without considering relevant material and without establishing that it serves mineral development.
material_facts: The State granted numerous second renewals in a short period, including after the proposed change to the mining-allocation framework became public.

The State did not await or consider the results of investigations it had initiated into lease-holder violations, despite its policy stating that such violations could exclude lease holders from renewal.
Reports documented widespread mining and environmental violations, and the State did not adequately consider those reports or the environmental degradation they described.
Goan iron ore was principally exported, with little domestic value addition, while the mining lease holders stood to gain commercially.
The State’s decision appeared directed at restoring revenue rather than being based on a holistic assessment of mineral development.
issues.conclusion: The second renewals were unduly hasty, failed to take relevant material into account, and were not in the interests of mineral development; they were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the MMDR Act requires the State to form an opinion that renewal is necessary in the interests of mineral development and to record reasons. Under Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1996) 9 SCC 709, mineral development must be considered holistically, including captive mining, industry requirements, and equitable distribution under Article 39(b). Article 14 permits limited review of executive decisions allocating natural resources. Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, (2012) 10 SCC 1, explains that allocation for private commercial profit without a social or welfare purpose may attract Article 14 scrutiny. The State’s own mining policy also made renewal contingent on considering investigations and violations.

rule.if: challenge_to_second_renewal and state_granted_renewals and relevant_investigations_unconsidered and material_violations_unconsidered and mineral_development_not_demonstrated

predicates.challenge_to_second_renewal: A proceeding challenges the State’s decision to grant second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.state_granted_renewals: The State granted second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.relevant_investigations_unconsidered: The State made renewal decisions without awaiting or considering investigations it had initiated into relevant conduct.
predicates.material_violations_unconsidered: The State did not adequately consider documented violations or other relevant environmental and mining evidence.
predicates.mineral_development_not_demonstrated: The State’s decision was not shown to rest on a reasoned assessment that renewal served mineral development.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges second renewals granted without considering relevant investigations and violations and without demonstrating mineral development, the renewals are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A mining lease grant or renewal requires a fresh environmental clearance, and an earlier clearance cannot by itself authorize the later grant or renewal.
material_facts: The earlier leases had expired, and the State was required to grant fresh mining leases.
Some operators relied on environmental clearances issued under the 1994 notification, while others relied on clearances under the 2006 notification.
The Court found that the 1994 clearances had a five-year validity and that a clearance was required when a lease was renewed.
The Court found that the 2006 clearances could remain valid for the estimated project life, subject to a maximum of thirty years, but a fresh lease still required a fresh clearance.
issues.conclusion: Fresh environmental clearances were required for fresh mining leases. A valid clearance under the 2006 notification did not need to be set aside merely because of its validity period, but a new clearance was required upon a fresh lease. The 1994 clearances did not remove the need for a fresh clearance at renewal and had expired by the relevant time.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Environment Impact Assessment Notification of 27 January 1994 and paragraph 9 of the Environment Impact Assessment Notification of 14 September 2006. It relied on M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2004) 12 SCC 118, which held that a mining operation requires environmental clearance and that a 1994 clearance is valid for five years, and Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499, which reaffirmed that renewal after 27 January 1994 requires clearance. The Court also relied on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, (1987) 1 SCC 213, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., 1989 Supp (1) SCC 504, and State of M.P. v. Krishnadas Tikaram, 1995 Supp (1) SCC 587, on compliance with statutory requirements at renewal. Under the 2006 notification, a mining-project clearance lasts for the estimated project life up to thirty years; that does not dispense with a fresh clearance for a fresh lease.

predicates.mining_project_requires_fresh_lease_or_r: A mining project is proceeding under a fresh lease or a renewed lease.
predicates.prior_clearance_relates_to_earlier_lease: The environmental clearance relied on was issued for an earlier lease or an earlier grant.

issues.definition: When a mining project proceeds under a fresh or renewed lease and its existing clearance relates to an earlier lease or grant, a fresh environmental clearance is required.

issues.legal_issue: An environmental authority cannot lift the suspension of environmental clearances mechanically without considering documented violations and relevant expert reports.
material_facts: The environmental authority lifted the suspension for a number of mines after the State requested it to do so.
The expert appraisal committee had documented multiple violations, including excess production, unauthorized dump mining, groundwater issues, encroachments, and missing clearances.
A court-appointed expert committee had reported large-scale environmental degradation.
The environmental authority’s decision did not adequately consider the violations or expert reports and instead largely deferred action to the State.
issues.conclusion: The environmental authority’s exercise in lifting the suspension was void because it was mechanical, lacked due application of mind, and failed to consider relevant material. The mining lease holders were required to obtain fresh environmental clearances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirements of reasoned administrative decision-making and environmental law, together with its directions in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738. It considered the reports of the Vishwanath Anand Expert Appraisal Committee and the Court-appointed Expert Committee, and the principles in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2004) 12 SCC 118, and Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499, concerning environmental clearance for mining and renewal. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the environmental assessment notifications governed the clearances and violations.

rule.if: challenge_to_lifting_environmental_suspension and documented_violations and expert_reports_not_considered and suspension_lifted_mechanically

predicates.challenge_to_lifting_environmental_suspe: A proceeding challenges an authority’s decision to lift the suspension of environmental clearances.
predicates.documented_violations: Expert or official material records significant violations by the project operators.
predicates.expert_reports_not_considered: The authority does not adequately consider relevant expert findings before deciding.
predicates.suspension_lifted_mechanically: The authority lifts the suspension without a substantive assessment of the relevant material.

issues.definition: When a challenged decision lifts an environmental suspension mechanically despite documented violations and without considering expert reports, the lifting is void.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot direct execution of second-renewal leases where a prior final judgment requires the State to grant fresh mining leases.
material_facts: A High Court directed the State to execute leases for some applicants and to decide other second-renewal applications.
The High Court relied in part on applicants’ timely applications, approved mining plans, payments, and promissory estoppel.
A prior final judgment of the Supreme Court required fresh mining leases rather than second renewals.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment and directions were set aside because they proceeded on an erroneous understanding of the prior Supreme Court judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The prior decision in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738, required fresh mining leases and did not authorize second renewals. A lower court’s directions cannot contradict that binding determination. The Court accordingly set aside the decision in Lithoferro v. State of Goa, MANU/MH/1292/2014, and rejected its interpretation of the earlier judgment.

predicates.appeal_challenges_renewal_direction: An appeal challenges a court order concerning renewal of mining leases.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_required_fresh_gran: A prior final judgment required fresh grants rather than renewals of expired leases.
predicates.lower_court_ordered_second_renewals: The lower court directed the State to execute or decide second-renewal leases.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a renewal direction that conflicts with a prior final requirement of fresh grants, the renewal direction must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Operators holding invalid second renewals may be allowed a temporary transition to manage their affairs before mining operations must cease pending fresh grants and clearances.
material_facts: The second renewals were quashed, but the operators needed time to manage their affairs.
The Court directed that mining operations cease after a temporary transition and remain stopped until fresh leases and environmental clearances were granted.
issues.conclusion: The operators were permitted to continue mining temporarily during the transition, but had to stop until fresh mining leases and environmental clearances were granted.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its remedial and case-management powers, the Court allowed a limited transition after quashing the renewals, while making clear that continued operations thereafter required fresh mining leases and environmental clearances. The direction implemented the Court’s conclusions in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738, and the environmental-clearance requirements under the applicable law.

predicates.invalid_second_renewals: The operators’ second renewals have been held invalid.
predicates.operators_need_transition: The operators require a transition to manage their affairs after the renewals are set aside.
predicates.fresh_grants_and_clearances_not_yet_obta: Fresh mining leases and environmental clearances have not yet been obtained.

issues.definition: When second renewals are invalid, operators need a transition, and replacement grants and clearances are not yet obtained, temporary continuation may be allowed before operations must stop.
